facts.quote: The anterior vertebrae of the tail were opisthocoelous, which means they were convex on their anterior sides and concave on their back sides, forming ball-and-socket joints.

facts.quote: The forelimbs measured 1.87 m in height in the nearly complete specimen, approximately two thirds the length of the hindlimbs, which were reconstructed at 2.46 m height.

facts.statement: The manus of Opisthocoelicaudia consisted of five vertically oriented metacarpalia arranged in a semicircle.
facts.quote: The manus was composed merely of the five metacarpalia, which were orientated vertically and arranged in a semicircle.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia completely lacked finger bones and claws, a feature more extreme than in most other titanosaurs.
facts.quote: Finger bones and claws were also completely absent – in most other titanosaurs, these bones were still present though extremely reduced in size.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of Opisthocoelicaudia is 2-2-2-1-0.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula, which states the number of phalanges (digit bones) beginning with the innermost digit, is 2-2-2-1-0.

facts.statement: In Opisthocoelicaudia, the first digit claw was roughly equal in size to the second digit claw, unlike in other sauropods where it is typically larger.
facts.quote: The claw of the first digit was not larger than that of the second digit, as in other sauropods, but roughly equal in size.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia was described by Borsuk-Białynicka in 1977.
facts.quote: Borsuk-Białynicka, in her 1977 description, noted the presence of eleven dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia was originally classified within the family Camarasauridae.
facts.quote: Originally, Opisthocoelicaudia was classified as a member of the family Camarasauridae, together with Camarasaurus and Euhelopus.

facts.statement: Leonardo Salgado and Rodolfo Coria classified Opisthocoelicaudia as a titanosaur within the family Titanosauridae in 1993.
facts.quote: In 1993, Leonardo Salgado and Rodolfo Coria showed Opisthocoelicaudia to represent a titanosaur and classified it within the family Titanosauridae.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia is closely related to Alamosaurus, Neuquensaurus, Rocasaurus, and Saltasaurus, forming the family Saltasauridae within the clade Lithostrotia.
facts.quote: Within the Lithostrotia, Opisthocoelicaudia has been found to be closely related to the genera Alamosaurus, Neuquensaurus, Rocasaurus and Saltasaurus, together forming the family Saltasauridae.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Opisthocoelicaudia and Alamosaurus form a monophyletic group called Opisthocoelicaudiinae or if this group is paraphyletic.
facts.quote: Many scientists considered Opisthocoelicaudia to be most closely related to Alamosaurus, with both genera forming a monophyletic group, the Opisthocoelicaudiinae. Other scientists concluded that the Opisthocoelicaudiinae is paraphyletic (not forming a natural group).

facts.statement: Upchurch and colleagues argued in 2004 that Alamosaurus is not related to Opisthocoelicaudia and should be placed outside the Saltasauridae.
facts.quote: Contradicting most other studies, Upchurch and colleagues in 2004 argued that Alamosaurus has to be placed outside the Saltasauridae as a close relative of Pellegrinisaurus, and therefore is not related to Opisthocoelicaudia at all.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia lacks a skull and neck, leading to suspicions that it might be a synonym of Nemegtosaurus.
facts.quote: Opisthocoelicaudia, on the other hand, lacks both the skull and neck, precluding a direct comparison and leading to suspicions that it may represent a synonym of Nemegtosaurus.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia was discovered during the 1965 joint Polish-Mongolian expedition.
facts.quote: Both Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus were discovered during the 1965 joint Polish-Mongolian expedition.

facts.statement: In 1977, Borsuk-Białynicka classified Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus as separate genera based on their presumed family affiliations.
facts.quote: In 1977, Borsuk-Białynicka deemed Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus to represent separate genera because Nemegtosaurus was at this time considered to be a member of the Dicraeosauridae, while Opisthocoelicaudia seemed to be a representative of a different group, the Camarasauridae.

facts.statement: Opisthocoelicaudia is classified within the Titanosauria.

facts.statement: In 2005, Jeffrey Wilson suggested that Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus might be synonyms.

facts.statement: Currie and colleagues argued in 2003 and 2017 that Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus are likely synonyms based on new fossil evidence.
facts.quote: Currie and colleagues, in 2003 and 2017, argued that a synonymy is very probable in the light of new fossil discoveries in the Nemegt Formation.

facts.statement: In 2019, Averianov and Lopatin argued that Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus are distinct genera based on differing fossil remains.
facts.quote: In 2019, Alexander O. Averianov and Alexey V. Lopatin reported Nemegt sauropod vertebrae discovered in 1949 and some femora that differed from the same bones of Opisthocoelicaudia, and stated they probably belonged to Nemegtosaurus, thereby supporting that the two genera were distinct.

facts.statement: Definitive proof that Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus are synonyms is still missing.
facts.quote: Definitive proof for the suggested synonymy is, however, still missing, and additional overlapping elements would be required before Opisthocoelicaudia and Nemegtosaurus can be formally declared synonyms.

facts.statement: Borsuk-Białynicka originally assumed Opisthocoelicaudia's neck was horizontal or slightly slanted downward.

facts.quote: Opisthocoelicaudia may have been able to rear up on its hindlimbs for foraging, using its tail as a third leg.

facts.statement: In 2005, Wilson hypothesized that rearing was an innovation shared by Opisthocoelicaudia and related Saltasaurinae genera.

facts.statement: Sauropod footprints from the Nemegt Formation were first described in 2003 by Currie and colleagues.

facts.statement: Currie and colleagues assigned sauropod tracks found in the Nemegt Formation to Opisthocoelicaudia, assuming Nemegtosaurus was a synonym.
facts.quote: The sauropod tracks were assigned to Opisthocoelicaudia, which, according to these authors, showed a matching hind foot morphology and was probably the only known sauropod (and, thus, the only potential trackmaker species) from the Nemegt Formation when Nemegtosaurus is regarded a synonym.
